I just want to work on a topic, an idea I had, or to be more precise, to let you work on this idea. I am going to give you some pointers. The topic is combinatorics on binary. It's an idea I've had for a very long time, and a quite dumb one or very naive one. But any binary code written in bytes, when you have the sequence, it always occurs to me that it's quite easy to have a sliding window on this sequence. The window is, of course, of a set length, let's say small omega. And when the window slides on this sequence, this binary sequence, of course it creates smaller size binary codes. Now our memory and numbers are using binary encoding to be represented. Which means that when one window slides on this sequence, depending on which part of the sequence the window reads, it produces a new number. And under the condition that the binary sequence on which the window slides can be fully scanned by the window with a number that can be expressed in bits that is slower, that is lower than the final number we can represent when you concatenate the results of the window reading the original binary sequence and sliding on it, then what we have is that we have encoded, we have compressed information because we have a way to generate bigger numbers by sliding the window on this original binary sequence. I feel like this is a very interesting combinatorics problem because all of this can be expressed in math. We can have definitely the upper and lower bounds of the numbers that can be imp- expressed for a given original sequence and a given window. And you have to see that as if we have this original sequence that we need to find a name for them, like generative sequence or cardinal sequences or something else. There should be a way to express how we can compress or how we can generate, depending the direction in which you are looking, where everything, a huge image, for instance, let's say, or for that matter, weights of language models or weights of neural networks in general, which are always very big, very large, could be stored at a very potentially inexpensive or compressed rates, simply if we have these original sequence plus windows going through that original sequence plus, of course, the position of the window spans. So as long as we can encode, as long as the size of the original sequence plus the sequence of window reads leads to a lower memory count than the original sequence, then we have saved something, we have compressed information. Simply because we rely on the patterns in the original sequence. I want you to work on this topic. You are not going to be the one to work on it directly. You are like a private investigator. You delegate work to your team, but you are also aware that your team, made of Sonnet agents, general agents, there is a cost to delegation. Because any delegation incurs drifts or possibly errors that the independent agent is going to do. And so anything that has errors means that it needs to be checked by a reviewer. But even if the agent does its work perfectly, there is the cost at the entry of delegating and the cost of getting back the information, you're reading it plus verifying. So there is a lot of communication cost here that has been already studied by information theory to some extent. It's not exactly the same, but it's very close. And so when you work with your team, you must keep in mind that everything has a cost when you communicate and everything has a cost when you delegate. And sometimes, just sometimes, you might realize that it's easier for you to do it or less costly, cheaper for you to do something rather than to delegate. Or it's cheaper for you to launch a loop between implementer and verifier where you just let two people, two agents discussing and reviewing each other's work, than to you ever actually reading the result. Sometimes you will have to fight against your wish to check everything that comes back to you simply because you have to trust that the other agent did it well. And of course, if there is any problem, then we can track it back to that other agent and you can send him back a message and reuse that agent that has already all the warm context so that it can correct its error. But you can trust your agent to some extent. To help you with these tasks and projects, I request that you leverage the skills that help you manage roadmaps. Don't make a huge roadmaps. You can divide subtopics of the roadmaps into sub-roadmaps, like having one roadmap which will help you um, that will help you lay out the general trajectory of the project. And then for each of the subparts of this project, probably you can have roadmaps and you can have a graph that way, a graph of roadmaps with dependencies. Then you also need to have very structured reports. And for this, I invite you to write, to use the skill telling you how to write reports. The findings, when there is any interesting result to bring back between or to travel between agents. The observations, the knowledge transfers, basically leverage any type of reports so that agents can communicate information in a very structured manner and everything will be tracked and pulled at the directory where the reports will be written. And finally, and probably the most important one, is that you must absolutely leverage segment semantic search. You have the callgrep MCP and the callgrep search skill. You can manage the indexes and you can create new indexes. You can prune them when you don't need them anymore. The point is that if you are going to work as a team, then the team needs to be able to find information reliably. And putting aside team management, you have access to the Wolfram Language MCP server, which gives you a lot of computational tools to do a lot of math, symbols definition, plots, generation, proofs, solving. But also, Wolfram Language can be a bit slow, or be careful at the things you are trying to solve, because my rule of thumb with this is that if Mathematica cannot compute it in less than 10 seconds, then definitely it's not the way to go at tackling the symbolic problems, or the symbolic problems needs to be redefined. Or the experiments need to be, the protocols need to be reworked. So go ahead. I don't have any major things. And that's already a lot of content. I want to emphasize that, again, you are a principal investigator. You are there to organize work. And you can do some of the work yourself. But I don't think there is anything in that project that will require my input because the topic is already defined and you already have the tool to study it.
